title: INTERACTIVE DASHBOARD
text:
In Looker Studio, interactivity helps stakeholders quickly focus on the information that matters most. This is especially useful when analyzing trends, comparing categories, or investigating performance across different segments.
By adding filters and navigation controls, dashboards become tools for data exploration, not just data display.

title: INTERACTIVE DASHBOARD
text:
1.1 Date Range Filter
A Date Range Filter allows users to dynamically change the time window displayed in a dashboard.
For example, users can switch between:

Last 7 days
Last 30 days
This year
Custom date ranges

This helps users quickly answer questions such as:

How did sales perform this month?
Is revenue growing compared to last quarter?

title: INTERACTIVE DASHBOARD
text:
2.1 Drop-down Filter
A Drop-down Filter allows users to select values from a list.
Common examples include filtering by:

Product category
Region
Brand or company
Property project

When a user selects a value from the drop-down filter, all connected charts update automatically.

title: INTERACTIVE DASHBOARD
text:
3.1 Segment Filtering
Segment filtering allows users to isolate specific groups of data for deeper analysis.
Examples include:

Viewing sales for a single region
Analyzing performance for one product category
Comparing results between customer segments

Segment filters allow decision-makers to quickly answer targeted questions without modifying the dataset.

title: INTERACTIVE DASHBOARD
text:
4.1 Cross-filtering
Cross-filtering enables charts to act as interactive filters.
For example:

Clicking on a product category in a bar chart filters other charts to show only that category.
Selecting a region updates revenue, demand, and KPI charts for that region.

This interaction helps users move quickly from high-level insights to detailed analysis.

title: INTERACTIVE DASHBOARD
text:
5.1 Interactive Navigation
Interactive navigation helps users move between different views or sections of a dashboard.
Examples include:

Navigating between overview and detailed analysis pages
Switching between sales and marketing dashboards
Exploring different product segments

Navigation controls help organize complex dashboards and make them easier to use.

title: LOOKER STUDIO FUNDAMENTALS
text:
Looker Studio is a business intelligence tool that helps transform raw data into clear and interactive dashboards. Instead of analyzing data directly from spreadsheets, analysts can visualize patterns, trends, and performance indicators in a structured way.
In business environments, dashboards are used to monitor KPIs, identify problems early, and support decision-making. Before building advanced dashboards, it is important to understand how data is connected, structured, and visualized in Looker Studio.

title: LOOKER STUDIO FUNDAMENTALS
text:
1.1 Connect Google Sheets
Google Sheets is one of the most commonly used data sources in Looker Studio. Many teams store operational data, reports, or exported system data in spreadsheets.






NoteTo connect a Google Sheet




Open Looker Studio and create a new report.
Click Add Data.
Select Google Sheets as the data source.
Choose the spreadsheet and worksheet that contains the dataset.
Confirm the connection.



Once connected, Looker Studio automatically detects the available fields and allows them to be used in charts, filters, and calculations.

title: LOOKER STUDIO FUNDAMENTALS
text:
1.2 Import Excel / CSV Files
In some situations, data may come from external systems in Excel or CSV format. These files can also be used in Looker Studio after being uploaded or converted.






NoteA common workflow




Upload the Excel or CSV file into Google Sheets.
Clean and verify the data structure.
Connect the spreadsheet to Looker Studio.

CSV files are often used when exporting large datasets from databases or operational systems.

title: LOOKER STUDIO FUNDAMENTALS
text:
2.1 Metrics vs Dimensions
Fields in Looker Studio are categorized into dimensions and metrics.
Dimensions describe categorical information. They answer the question “what or which?”,
Examples:

Region
Product
Property Project
Sales Channel
Date


Metrics represent numerical values that can be measured and aggregated.
Examples:

Revenue
Number of Units Sold
Leads Generated
Marketing Cost

For Example:



Dimension
Metric




Project Name
Revenue


Region
Units Sold


Month
Marketing Spend









Note



Dimensions group the data, while metrics provide the values being analyzed.

title: LOOKER STUDIO FUNDAMENTALS
text:
2.2 Aggregation Logic
Metrics are usually calculated using aggregation functions. Aggregation determines how multiple records are summarized in a chart.

SUM

Adds all values together.
Example: total revenue across projects.

AVG (Average)

Calculates the average value.
Example: average marketing cost per campaign.

COUNT

Counts the number of records.
Example: number of transactions.


Choosing the correct aggregation ensures that the dashboard reflects the real performance of the business.

Incorrect aggregation can lead to misleading insights.

title: LOOKER STUDIO FUNDAMENTALS
text:
3.1 Basic Chart Types
Choosing the right chart is important because different charts serve different analytical purposes. Below are several common chart types that are widely used in Looker Studio dashboards.
Example dataset:







3.1.1 Bar Chart
Bar charts are used to compare values across different categories. They are one of the most commonly used charts in business dashboards.








3.1.2 Line Chart
Line charts are used to visualize trends or ordered comparisons. Since this dataset does not contain time variables, we can use the chart to compare average selling price across companies.








3.1.3 Pie Chart / Doughnut Chart
Pie charts show how different categories contribute to a total.








3.1.4 Scatter Plot
Scatter plots help analyze relationships between two numerical variables.








3.1.5 Histogram
Histograms show how frequently values fall within certain ranges. This helps analysts understand the distribution of a dataset.








3.1.6 Area Chart
Area charts are similar to line charts but emphasize the magnitude of change over time.








3.1.7 Scorecard
Scorecards display a single KPI value with optional comparison indicators.

title: LOOKER STUDIO FUNDAMENTALS
text:
3.2 Chart Configuration
After selecting a chart type, it is important to configure it correctly to ensure accurate reporting.
Key chart settings include:

Dimension Selection → Defines how data is grouped.
Metric Selection → Determines what values are displayed.
Sorting → Controls the order of data, such as ranking projects by revenue.
Date Range → Limits the data to a specific time period.
Labels and Titles →Provide context so users understand what the chart represents.

Proper configuration ensures that charts present reliable and meaningful information for decision-making.

title: DASHBOARD DESIGN
text: A well-designed dashboard helps users understand data quickly and accurately. Good design is not only about visual appearance but also about how information is structured and prioritized. In this section, participants will learn how to apply design principles that improve readability, clarity, and insight delivery in a dashboard.

title: DASHBOARD DESIGN
text:
1.1 Theme Application
Looker Studio provides predefined themes that can be applied directly to a report. These themes include predefined color palettes, typography settings, and chart styles that automatically format the dashboard layout.
Looker Studio provides a set of default themes that any user can apply without deep configuration. To use one:






NoteUse themes in Looker Studio




Open your report in Edit mode
In the top menu bar, click File > Theme and layout
In the right-hand panel, open the Theme tab
Choose one of the standard themes from the list



That’s it. The selected theme will automatically apply to your report.

If the automatically generated theme isn’t perfect or requires adjustments, you can manually tweak each part of it. To do this:

Select the theme you want to edit
Click Customize at the top of the panel

You can then adjust:

Main colors (accent, background, text, axes, etc.)
Fonts (global and per element type)
Chart styles (background color, border style, transparency, corner shape, layout, and more)

Once you achieve the desired visual result, your theme setup is complete.

title: DASHBOARD DESIGN
text:
2.1 Font Hierarchy
In a dashboard, not all information should have the same visual emphasis. Titles, key metrics, and labels should have different sizes and weights so users can easily understand the structure of the report.









Level
Purpose
Example




Title
Dashboard or section heading
“Monthly Sales Dashboard”


Metric
Important KPIs
Revenue, Conversion Rate


Label
Supporting information
Category, Date, Region





2.1.1 Applying Font Hierarchy
In Looker Studio, font settings can be adjusted through the Theme and Layout panel or directly within each chart component.
Basic steps to modify typography:

Select a chart or text element.
Open the Style panel on the right side.
Choose the font family, font size, and font weight.
Apply consistent settings across titles, metrics, and labels.


Typography in dashboards is like good plumbing – when it’s done right, nobody notices it, but when it’s wrong, everything breaks down.
Font Hierarchy Guidelines:

Headers: 24-32px, bold weight, short and descriptive
Subheaders: 16-20px, medium weight, contextual information
Body/Data: 12-14px, regular weight, high readability
Annotations: 10-12px, light weight, supplementary details

Font Choice: Stick to system fonts or widely supported web fonts. Avoid decorative fonts in data contexts – readability trumps personality every time.

title: DASHBOARD DESIGN
text:
3.1 Primary vs Accent Colors
Color hierarchy in dashboards typically consists of primary colors and accent colors. Each color plays a different role in guiding user attention.

3.1.1 Primary Colors
